```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = FALSE, warning = FALSE, message = FALSE,
  fig.pos = "!ht", collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
if (knitr::is_latex_output()) knitr::opts_chunk$set(dev = "cairo_pdf")
# Display helper: round once to four decimals and drop trailing zeros;
# a vector shares the fewest decimals that show every member.
num4 <- function(x) format(round(x, 4), digits = 15, scientific = FALSE,
  trim = TRUE)
sound_levels <- c("Silence", "Instrumental music", "Music with lyrics")
sound_data <- data.frame(
  student = sprintf("S%02d", 1:30),
  sound = factor(rep(sound_levels, each = 10), levels = sound_levels),
  score = c(8, 9, 9, 11, 12, 13, 13, 14, 15, 16,
            6, 8, 8, 9, 9, 11, 11, 12, 12, 14,
            4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 8, 9, 10, 11, 12))
one_way <- aov(score ~ sound, data = sound_data)
feedback_data <- data.frame(
  student = 1:24,
  feedback = factor(rep(c("Rereading", "Answer feedback",
    "Explanatory feedback"), each = 8),
    levels = c("Rereading", "Answer feedback", "Explanatory feedback")),
  practice = factor(rep(rep(c("Massed", "Spaced"), each = 4), 3),
    levels = c("Massed", "Spaced")),
  score = c(4, 5, 7, 8, 4, 5, 7, 8,
    6, 7, 9, 10, 10, 11, 13, 14,
    8, 9, 11, 12, 16, 17, 19, 20))
full_fit <- aov(score ~ feedback * practice, data = feedback_data)
```

```{r}
#| label: ch04-oneway-check
#| include: false
# Stops the render if a printed one-way anchor no longer matches its data.
f4 <- function(x) sprintf("%.4f", x)
one_way_table <- anova(one_way)
welch_check <- oneway.test(score ~ sound, data = sound_data,
  var.equal = FALSE)
tukey_check <- TukeyHSD(one_way, which = "sound")$sound
two_groups <- droplevels(subset(sound_data, sound != "Instrumental music"))
t_two <- t.test(score ~ sound, data = two_groups, var.equal = TRUE)
group_mean <- ave(sound_data$score, sound_data$sound)
doubled_check <- anova(aov(score ~ sound, data = transform(sound_data,
  score = group_mean + 2 * (score - group_mean))))
stopifnot(
  f4(tapply(sound_data$score, sound_data$sound, sd)) ==
    c("2.7080", "2.4037", "2.5820"),
  f4(one_way_table$`F value`[1]) == "6.0674",
  f4(one_way_table$`Pr(>F)`[1]) == "0.0067",
  f4(one_way_table$`Mean Sq`[2]) == "6.5926",
  f4(c(welch_check$statistic, welch_check$parameter[2],
    welch_check$p.value)) == c("5.5144", "17.9561", "0.0136"),
  f4(tukey_check[, "lwr"]) == c("-4.8470", "-6.8470", "-4.8470"),
  f4(tukey_check[, "upr"]) == c("0.8470", "-1.1530", "0.8470"),
  f4(tukey_check[, "p adj"]) == c("0.2085", "0.0047", "0.2085"),
  f4(c(t_two$statistic, t_two$p.value)) == c("3.3806", "0.0033"),
  f4(c(doubled_check$`F value`[1], doubled_check$`Pr(>F)`[1])) ==
    c("1.5169", "0.2375"))
# Anchors of the what-moves-F table, the F-reference figure, the
# familywise figure, the printed family critical values and the
# practice-ignored display.
gm <- ave(sound_data$score, sound_data$sound)
halved <- transform(sound_data, score = score - (gm - 10) / 2)
halved_tab <- anova(aov(score ~ sound, data = halved))
v <- tapply(sound_data$score, sound_data$sound, var)
F_twenty <- (20 * 8 / 2) / (19 * sum(v) / 57)
critical <- c(qt(.975, 27), qt(1 - .05 / 4, 27), sqrt(2 * qf(.95, 2, 27)))
F_crit <- c(qf(.95, 2, 27), qf(.95, 2, 8), qf(.95, 5, 27))
m <- 1:10
se_pair <- sqrt(178 / 27 * (1 / 10 + 1 / 10))
ignore_tab <- anova(aov(score ~ feedback, data = feedback_data))
stopifnot(
  f4(c(halved_tab$`Mean Sq`[1], halved_tab$`F value`[1],
    halved_tab$`Pr(>F)`[1])) == c("10.0000", "1.5169", "0.2375"),
  f4(c(F_twenty, 160 / (160 + 19 * sum(v)))) == c("12.1348", "0.2986"),
  pf(F_twenty, 2, 57, lower.tail = FALSE) < .0001,
  f4(critical) == c("2.0518", "2.3734", "2.5900"),
  f4(c(-2, -4) - critical[2] * se_pair) == c("-4.7253", "-6.7253"),
  f4(c(-2, -4) + critical[2] * se_pair) == c("0.7253", "-1.2747"),
  f4(F_crit) == c("3.3541", "4.4590", "2.5719"),
  f4(1 - (1 - .05)^c(3, 5)) == c("0.1426", "0.2262"),
  all(1 - (1 - .05 / m)^m <= .05 + 1e-12),
  f4(c(ignore_tab$`Mean Sq`[2], ignore_tab$`F value`[1],
    ignore_tab$`Pr(>F)`[1])) == c("10.4762", "12.2182", "0.0003"),
  f4(tapply(feedback_data$score, feedback_data$feedback, sd)) ==
    c("1.6903", "2.7255", "4.5981"),
  f4(258 / 29) == "8.8966")
# Anchors of Section 4.7: the familywise rate at seven tests and the
# counts of tbl-ch04-multiway.
k <- 2:4
cells <- c(6, 12, 24)
stopifnot(
  f4(1 - (1 - .05)^7) == "0.3017",
  2^k - 1 == c(3, 7, 15),
  4 * cells - cells == c(18, 36, 72),
  choose(12, 2) == 66)
```

\clearpage

::: {.callout-note title="Chapter overview"}
This chapter compares means by examining variation. Two invented studies
provide the observations: a one-way experiment on background sound while
studying carries the first analyses, and a two-factor experiment
crossing feedback with practice schedule carries the factorial analysis,
which asks how a comparison changes across practice schedules. We follow
the one-way ANOVA from individual scores to its F distribution, distinguish its
omnibus question from a particular contrast, and explain how the
comparison family determines an interval's coverage. Cell means and
simple effects then reveal what main effects can conceal, and a closing
look at three and four factors shows how a two-way pattern can itself
change. By the end,
you will be able to read an ANOVA table and the F distribution behind
it, interpret a contrast and its uncertainty within a family of
comparisons, and connect a factorial pattern to the design and model
conditions that support its interpretation.
:::

Two **invented studies** supply the observations. In the first, thirty
first-year university students each read the same passage for 20
minutes and then answer a 20-item reading-comprehension quiz, scored
from 0 to 20. Each student reads in an individual session and is
randomly assigned to one of three background-sound conditions, ten to
each: *Silence*, *Instrumental music*, or *Music with lyrics* playing
during the reading. In the second, twenty-four students study the same
fractions material and complete a common 20-item quiz. Random
allocation places four different students in each combination of three
feedback conditions and two practice schedules. *Rereading* offers the
worked material again; *Answer feedback* supplies the correct answer
after an attempt; *Explanatory feedback* supplies the answer with a
worked explanation. *Massed* practice occurs in one session and
*Spaced* practice in two shorter sessions with the same total practice
time. Everyone completes the quiz at the same specified follow-up point
after their final practice. These design details and all scores are
invented for teaching.

Our first question concerns the background-sound study: how do the
three sound-condition means compare? Chapter 3 built, step by step, the
tools for one comparison: an estimate and its standard error, a
confidence interval, a hypothesis test with its p-value, and the t tests
for one sample, paired samples and two independent samples. For two
independent groups sharing one spread, the equal-variance t test pooled
the two group variances. We extend that reasoning to several groups,
keeping the difference between an overall pattern and particular
comparisons visible.

Our later question concerns the feedback-by-practice study: how does
the feedback comparison depend on practice schedule? The number of
factors, not the number of groups, separates the two analyses. The
first study has one factor with three levels; the second has two
crossed factors forming six cells.

## Comparison Questions and Designs {#sec-ch04-design}

### Outcome, factors, cells and units

Both outcomes count correct answers. A comprehension score is the
number of reading-comprehension items answered correctly, and a quiz
score is the number of fractions items answered correctly; each runs
from 0 to 20, and higher values mean more correct answers. A four-point
difference therefore means four more correct answers on average; it
does not by itself describe every aspect of reading comprehension or of
learning fractions. The outcome and its scale give a numerical
comparison its substantive meaning.

A **factor** in analysis of variance is a categorical variable defining
groups or conditions. Its categories are **levels**. Background sound
has three levels. In the second study, feedback has three levels and
practice schedule has two. This use of *factor* differs from a latent
factor used to represent shared indicator variation in a measurement
model.

\Needspace{10\baselineskip}

| Sound condition | Comprehension scores of ten different students |
|:--|:--|
| Silence | 8, 9, 9, 11, 12, 13, 13, 14, 15, 16 |
| Instrumental music | 6, 8, 8, 9, 9, 11, 11, 12, 12, 14 |
| Music with lyrics | 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 8, 9, 10, 11, 12 |

: Invented reading-comprehension scores, ten different students per sound condition, on a 0--20 scale. {#tbl-ch04-sound-scores tbl-colwidths="[30,70]"}

One factor with three levels gives a **one-way** layout of three
groups. Each score in @tbl-ch04-sound-scores belongs to a different
student: the ten scores of one sound condition describe ten different
students, not repeated measurements, and the student is both the
stipulated assignment unit and the measurement unit. The scores are
fixed teaching values. They place the three group means two points
apart with similar, unequal spreads, so every calculation reproduces by
hand, but they do not establish a Normal model, equal variances or a
real effect of background sound.

The complete course data file, `background_sound.csv`, represents the
same table in one row per student, with columns `student`, `sound` and
`score`. Students are numbered S01--S30, ten to each sound condition in
the order Silence, Instrumental music, Music with lyrics. Silence is the
reference condition for the comparisons in Section 3.

A **cell** contains cases sharing one level of each factor. Answer
feedback with Spaced practice is one cell. Crossing three feedback
levels with two practice levels gives six cells, a **two-way** layout.
Four students per cell makes this layout **balanced**, as ten students
per condition balance the one-way layout. One-way and two-way refer to
the number of factors, not to the number of levels. A one-way analysis
can compare three, four or more groups, and a third or fourth crossed
factor gives a three-way or four-way layout (Section 4.7).

\Needspace{10\baselineskip}

| Feedback condition | Massed practice | Spaced practice |
|:--|:--|:--|
| Rereading | 4, 5, 7, 8 | 4, 5, 7, 8 |
| Answer feedback | 6, 7, 9, 10 | 10, 11, 13, 14 |
| Explanatory feedback | 8, 9, 11, 12 | 16, 17, 19, 20 |

: Invented fractions-quiz scores, four different students per cell, on a 0--20 scale. {#tbl-ch04-feedback-scores tbl-colwidths="[38,31,31]"}

Each score in @tbl-ch04-feedback-scores belongs to a different student.
The student is both the stipulated assignment unit and the measurement
unit. The four scores in a cell are not repeated measurements on one
student; nor are the Massed and Spaced scores paired. The repeated
within-cell pattern deliberately simplifies the arithmetic. It is a
teaching construction, not evidence of Normal errors, equal variances
or an educational effect.

The complete course data file, `feedback_practice.csv`, represents the
same table in one row per student, with columns `student`, `feedback`,
`practice` and `score`. Students are numbered 1--24, ordered by feedback,
then practice, then student within each cell. The printed scores in the
two tables are sufficient for every calculation in this chapter.

### Two studies, two questions

For the first analysis, the background-sound study has three groups
defined by one factor. Their model means, written $\mu_S$, $\mu_I$ and
$\mu_L$, refer to Silence, Instrumental music and Music with lyrics.
For example, $\mu_L-\mu_S$ states a direction and an outcome scale: how
many more or fewer comprehension items students answer correctly, on
average, with lyrics playing than in silence. The observed difference
estimates this particular contrast under the model introduced below.

The feedback-by-practice study crosses two factors, so its six cells
support a second kind of question: does the feedback comparison change
with practice schedule? Section 4 answers it with all 24 students.

\Needspace{16\baselineskip}

| Analysis | Records used | Question addressed |
|:--|:--|:--|
| One-way | Background-sound study: 30 students in three sound conditions, ten per condition | Do the mean comprehension scores differ across the three sound conditions? |
| Two-way | Feedback-by-practice study: 24 students in six feedback-by-practice cells, four per cell | What are the average factor comparisons, and how do comparisons change across the other factor? |

: Two questions, each asked of its own invented study. {#tbl-ch04-layouts tbl-colwidths="[16,40,44]"}

A two-factor ANOVA and the two-way frequency table of Chapter 3,
Section 6, have different outcomes. ANOVA compares a numerical score
across factor combinations. A frequency table counts cases in
combinations of categories. The word
*two-way* describes a layout; it does not identify a shared statistical
test.

### Design determines the relevant comparison

Random allocation is stipulated in each invented story. If implemented
in a real study, that design could support a causal comparison among
the participating students, subject to adherence, relevant interference
and missing outcomes. It would not make the participants a random sample
of all students. The data table alone establishes neither implementation
of assignment nor representativeness.

Different designs can produce superficially similar tables. If students
who heard one sound condition read together in one room, they would
share that session's influences, such as noise from a corridor or a
disruption partway through the reading. If whole classes receive
conditions, students within the same class may share influences and
the class may be the assignment unit. If each student is measured
twice, the two outcomes belong to a pair. For a real study, identify
the allocation, any repeated measurements, shared sessions or classroom
clustering, and any losses before choosing the error term. An
uncertainty formula must reflect these connections rather than treating
every row as an independent assignment.

**Blocking** makes condition comparisons within groups of similar
units. Chapter 3, Section 2.3, illustrates it with paired schools: in
each of twelve schools one class is assigned to each format, so the uncertainty
follows twelve independent within-school comparisons rather than 480
students. The three sound conditions and the six feedback-by-practice
cells in this chapter instead contain distinct, individually assigned
students.
Sampling strata, which organize selection into a sample, and allocation
blocks, which organize treatment comparisons, have different roles.

\Needspace{12\baselineskip}

## One-Way ANOVA {#sec-mean-comparison}

### Inspect grouped observations before reducing them

The three sound conditions have means 12, 10 and 8
comprehension points. Each has ten scores, and the sample SDs, 2.7080,
2.4037 and 2.5820, are similar. The ranges overlap widely: some
students who read with lyrics playing, scoring 11 or 12, outscored
some who read in silence, scoring 8 or 9. A difference between means
summarizes group distributions; it does not say that every student in
one group outperformed every student in another.

\Needspace{12\baselineskip}

| Sound condition | n | Mean | SD | Range |
|:--|--:|--:|--:|:--|
| Silence | 10 | 12 | 2.7080 | 8--16 |
| Instrumental music | 10 | 10 | 2.4037 | 6--14 |
| Music with lyrics | 10 | 8 | 2.5820 | 4--12 |

: Descriptions of the thirty background-sound scores. {#tbl-ch04-group-summary tbl-colwidths="[36,10,18,18,18]"}

@fig-ch04-separation-spread draws the same thirty scores in its left
panel: each box shows a group's median and middle half, and the points
keep every student visible, which a bar chart of the three means would
hide. That within-group variation matters to inference, because the
same distance between group means can be more or less convincing
depending on how widely individual scores vary within groups. The right
panel makes the point by construction: it doubles every score's
distance from its group mean, so the group means and counts stay fixed
while the spread doubles.

```{r}
#| label: fig-ch04-separation-spread
#| fig-cap: "The idea of ANOVA: the same group means with different within-group spread. Left: the thirty invented scores. Right: a constructed version in which every score's distance from its group mean is doubled, so the group means and counts are unchanged, although the medians that the boxes mark can shift. Boxes show each group's median and middle half; each point is a student, jittered sideways so that equal scores stay visible. Each panel's F statistic and p-value appear beneath it."
#| fig-alt: "Two panels of vertical boxplots with jittered points for Silence, Instrumental music and Music with lyrics. In the left panel the invented scores span 4 to 16, with medians 12.5, 10 and 8, and F(2, 27) = 6.0674, p = .0067 is printed beneath. In the right panel every deviation from the group mean is doubled, so the scores span 0 to 20, the boxes are about twice as tall and the Silence median moves to 13, while the group means stay at 12, 10 and 8, and F(2, 27) = 1.5169, p = .2375 is printed beneath."
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 3.8
#| out-width: 100%
group_mean <- ave(sound_data$score, sound_data$sound)
doubled <- transform(sound_data,
  score = group_mean + 2 * (score - group_mean))
p_text <- function(p) sub("^0", "", num4(p))
panel <- function(dat, title) {
  tab <- anova(aov(score ~ sound, data = dat))
  boxplot(score ~ sound, data = dat, ylim = c(0, 20), las = 1,
    names = c("Silence", "Instrumental", "Lyrics"),
    col = "grey92", border = "grey40", xlab = "", cex.axis = .85,
    ylab = "Comprehension score (0-20)", main = title)
  set.seed(12345)
  stripchart(score ~ sound, data = dat, vertical = TRUE,
    method = "jitter", jitter = .12, pch = 16, cex = .7,
    add = TRUE)
  mtext(sprintf("F(2, 27) = %s, p = %s", num4(tab[1, "F value"]),
    p_text(tab[1, "Pr(>F)"])), side = 1, line = 3.2)
}
par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(4.6, 4.2, 2.6, 1), cex.main = 1)
panel(sound_data, "Invented scores")
panel(doubled, "Same means, deviations doubled")
par(mfrow = c(1, 1))
```

Doubling every distance from the group mean multiplies its square by
four, so the within-group squared variation quadruples while the
separation of the means is unchanged.
The group SDs double, from 2.7080, 2.4037 and 2.5820 to 5.4160, 4.8074
and 5.1640. That change alone moves the F statistic printed beneath
each panel from 6.0674 to 1.5169, one quarter of its value, and the
p-value from .0067 to .2375: the same two-point steps between the means
stand out against narrow within-group spread and are lost in wide
spread. ANOVA compares these two kinds of variation after putting them
on comparable scales [@cetinkaya2024; @kutner2005]. Section 2.3
develops the F statistic and its p-value, and returns to this figure
with the two other quantities that move F.

### Mean model and the partition of variation

Write $Y_{ij}$ for the random score of student $i$ in sound condition $j$.
Here $j$ indexes a group, rather than a data-file column. The one-way
model is

$$
Y_{ij}=\mu_j+\varepsilon_{ij}.
$$

The unknown $\mu_j$ is the group mean in the model, and
$\varepsilon_{ij}$ is that student's unknown departure from it. After
fitting the group means, the **fitted value** is
$\widehat y_{ij}=\bar y_j$, and the **residual** is
$e_{ij}=y_{ij}-\bar y_j$. A residual is calculated from observed scores
and fitted means; a model error is a departure from an unknown model
mean. This distinction will recur in regression.

The observed grand mean is $\bar y=10$, the average of the three
group means because the groups are equally sized. Every score's
distance from the grand mean splits into two parts, the group's
departure from the grand mean and the student's residual:

$$
y_{ij}-\bar y=(\bar y_j-\bar y)+(y_{ij}-\bar y_j).
$$

For the Music-with-lyrics student who scored 4, $4-10=(8-10)+(4-8)$:
the group mean lies two points below the grand mean, and this student
another four points below the group mean. The first part is shared by
every student in the group; the second differs from student to
student.

[]{#app-ch04-small-data}Squaring the parts and adding over all thirty
students turns the split into a partition of the total squared
variation, $SS_T=SS_B+SS_W$, where

$$
\begin{aligned}
SS_T&=\sum_{j=1}^J\sum_{i=1}^{n_j}(y_{ij}-\bar y)^2,\\
SS_B&=\sum_{j=1}^Jn_j(\bar y_j-\bar y)^2,\\
SS_W&=\sum_{j=1}^J\sum_{i=1}^{n_j}(y_{ij}-\bar y_j)^2.
\end{aligned}
$$

The **total sum of squares** $SS_T$ measures variation around the one
grand mean. The **between-group sum of squares** $SS_B$ counts each
group's departure once for every student in that group, so it grows as
the group means separate. The **within-group sum of squares** $SS_W$
adds the squared residuals around the group means. The partition holds
because, within each group, the cross-products
$2(\bar y_j-\bar y)(y_{ij}-\bar y_j)$ sum to zero: the group's departure
is the same for every student, and the residuals of a group sum to zero.
For the background-sound study, $SS_B=80$, $SS_W=178$ and
$SS_T=258$, in squared comprehension points. The Instrumental-music
group adds nothing to $SS_B$, because its mean equals the grand mean,
although its scores still vary. The partition is arithmetic; it needs no
Normality or independence assumption. Those conditions enter when the
partition is used for inference, in Section 2.3.

### Degrees of freedom, mean squares and the F test {#sec-ch04-f-test}

A sum of squares grows with both the size of the departures and the
number of them, so each is divided by its **degrees of freedom** (df),
the number of departures that can vary freely, before the two sources
are compared. The F statistic has two kinds of df.

- The **between-groups df**, $J-1=2$, are the numerator df. The three
  group means can take any values, but once the grand mean is fixed
  their departures from it, weighted by group size, sum to zero, so
  only two of them are free.
- The **within-groups df**, $N-J=27$, are the denominator df. The ten
  residuals of each group sum to zero, so nine of them are free in each
  group, and three groups give 27.

The two kinds add to the total df, $N-1=29$, because the thirty
departures from the grand mean sum to zero. Dividing each sum of squares
by its df gives a **mean square**,

$$
MS_B=\frac{SS_B}{J-1},\qquad MS_W=\frac{SS_W}{N-J},\qquad
F=\frac{MS_B}{MS_W}.
$$

@tbl-ch04-one-way-anova gathers the parts.

\Needspace{9\baselineskip}

| Source | SS | df | What the df count | MS | F | p |
|:--|--:|--:|:--|--:|--:|--:|
| Sound condition | 80 | 2 | Group means free to vary, $J-1$ | 40.0000 | 6.0674 | .0067 |
| Within groups | 178 | 27 | Residuals free to vary after fitting three means, $N-J$ | 6.5926 | | |
| Total | 258 | 29 | Departures from the grand mean free to vary, $N-1$ | | | |

: One-way ANOVA for the 30 students of the background-sound study, with what each df counts. {#tbl-ch04-one-way-anova tbl-colwidths="[20,10,5,39,10,9,7]"}

[]{#sec-ch04-anova-table}Read the table as one sentence about the
observations, $\text{Data}=\text{fit}+\text{residual}$. The
sound-condition row is the fit, what the three group means account for;
the within-groups row is the residual, what is left around them; and the
total row is the data, measured around the grand mean. The sums of
squares add across the rows, $80+178=258$, and so do the df, $2+27=29$,
which makes a quick check of any printed table. $MS_W=6.5926$ estimates
the common error variance of the model; it is smaller than the total
sample variance, $258/29=8.8966$, because it leaves out the separation
of the means. Statistical software fits the same model from the thirty
records and often prints a longer layout, with rows such as an intercept
and an uncorrected total that serve the fitting rather than the
comparison question; the Computer Lab reads one such layout row by row.

The omnibus null hypothesis is $H_0:\mu_S=\mu_I=\mu_L$. The alternative
says that at least two of these means differ. Judging whether 6.0674 is
large needs the distribution that the statistic would follow if the null
were true.

Three conditions support this reference distribution, stated first in
familiar words. **Independent observations**: one student's departure
from a group mean carries no information about another student's
departure. Here that rests on the design, with students individually
assigned, each reading in an individual session and scored once; no
display of the scores can establish it. **Approximately Normal
residuals**: the departures around each group mean, not the pooled
mixture of all thirty scores, have a roughly Normal shape. **Similar
variances within groups**: one error variance $\sigma^2$ describes
every group, which is what allows $MS_W$ to pool the three group
variances. In model shorthand, the errors $\varepsilon_{ij}$ are
independent Normal with mean zero and common variance $\sigma^2$.

Under the null, both mean squares estimate the same error variance, so
their ratio tends to lie near 1; the numerator also grows with the
separation of the model means, so a large ratio is evidence against
equality. Under the three conditions and the null, F follows an
**F distribution**, one of a family of right-skewed distributions on
positive values, each indexed by its two df, numerator first: here
$F(2,27)$. The left panel of @fig-ch04-f-reference shows three members
of the family and marks each one's 5% point, the value beyond which 5%
of the distribution lies. With few denominator df, as in $F(2,8)$, the
error variance is poorly estimated and large ratios occur more often by
chance: its curve looks much like that of $F(2,27)$, but its heavier
tail moves the 5% point from 3.3541 to 4.4590. With more numerator df,
as in $F(5,27)$, the distribution gathers near 1 and its 5% point falls
to 2.5719.

```{r}
#| label: fig-ch04-f-reference
#| fig-cap: "F distributions and the one-way statistic. Left: three F distributions, each indexed by its numerator and denominator df; a vertical mark in each curve's colour and line type, labelled with its value, shows the point beyond which 5% of that distribution lies. Right: the right tail of F(2, 27), enlarged. The shaded areas together are the .05 beyond the critical value 3.3541; the dark area beyond the observed statistic 6.0674 is the p-value, .0067."
#| fig-alt: "Left panel, titled F distributions and 5% points: three right-skewed density curves over F values from 0 to 6. F(2, 27) and F(2, 8) both start near 1 at zero and decline almost together, F(2, 8) with a slightly heavier right tail; F(5, 27) rises from zero to a peak of about 0.73 near 0.6 and then declines. A labelled vertical mark in each curve's colour and line type stands at its 5% point: 2.5719 for F(5, 27), 3.3541 for F(2, 27) and 4.4590 for F(2, 8), so the heavier tail of F(2, 8) shows as a mark further to the right. Right panel: the F(2, 27) density from 2 to 9 on a vertical scale enlarged to 0.10. A dotted line marks the critical value 3.3541 and the area to its right is shaded light grey; a dashed line marks the observed F = 6.0674, and the dark area to its right is labelled p = .0067."
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 3.3
#| out-width: 100%
F_obs <- summary(one_way)[[1]][1, "F value"]
F_crit <- qf(.95, 2, 27)
df_pairs <- list(c(2, 27), c(2, 8), c(5, 27))
curve_col <- c("black", "#1F5A94", "#9B4922")
crit <- sapply(df_pairs, function(d) qf(.95, d[1], d[2]))
mark_top <- c(.34, .22, .46)
par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(4, 4.2, 2.4, .8), cex.main = .95)
xx <- seq(.001, 6, length.out = 600)
plot(NA, xlim = c(0, 6), ylim = c(0, 1), las = 1, xlab = "F statistic",
  ylab = "Density", main = "F distributions and 5% points")
for (k in 1:3) lines(xx, df(xx, df_pairs[[k]][1], df_pairs[[k]][2]),
  lwd = 2, lty = k, col = curve_col[k])
segments(crit, 0, crit, mark_top, lwd = 2, lty = 1:3, col = curve_col)
text(crit + .06, mark_top, num4(crit), adj = c(0, .3),
  col = curve_col, cex = .8)
legend("topright", lwd = 2, lty = 1:3, col = curve_col, bty = "n",
  cex = .8, sprintf("F(%d, %d)", sapply(df_pairs, `[`, 1),
    sapply(df_pairs, `[`, 2)))
xt <- seq(2, 9, length.out = 400)
plot(xt, df(xt, 2, 27), type = "n", ylim = c(0, .1), las = 1,
  xlab = "F statistic", ylab = "Density",
  main = "Right tail of F(2, 27), enlarged")
t1 <- seq(F_crit, 9, length.out = 200)
polygon(c(F_crit, t1, 9), c(0, df(t1, 2, 27), 0), col = "grey85",
  border = NA)
t2 <- seq(F_obs, 9, length.out = 200)
polygon(c(F_obs, t2, 9), c(0, df(t2, 2, 27), 0), col = "grey30",
  border = NA)
lines(xt, df(xt, 2, 27), lwd = 2)
segments(c(F_crit, F_obs), 0, c(F_crit, F_obs), c(.075, .035),
  lty = c(3, 2))
text(F_crit, .08, paste("Critical value", num4(F_crit)), adj = c(0, 0),
  cex = .75)
text(F_obs + .1, .04, sprintf("Observed\nF = %s\np = .0067", num4(F_obs)),
  adj = c(0, 0), cex = .75)
par(mfrow = c(1, 1))
```

The dark area in the right panel of @fig-ch04-f-reference, .0067, is
read in the same way as the tail areas and p-values of Chapter 3,
Section 4. Only the right tail counts, because greater separation of the
means produces a larger ratio. Under the null and the model conditions,
a ratio at least as large as 6.0674 occurs with that probability. The
observed F lies beyond the critical value 3.3541, so at a prespecified
.05 significance level the equality null is rejected; comparing F with
the critical value and comparing p with .05 give the same decision. This
is evidence about the three-mean pattern, not a probability that the
null is true and not an identification of which particular comparisons
differ.

The box below states, in the four lines used since Chapter 3, what this
F test addresses, what it rests on, what the data can check and what the
result supports.

[]{#ch04-justify-oneway}

::: {.callout-tip title="Justifying the analysis"}
- **Target:** whether the model means of the three sound conditions,
  $\mu_S$, $\mu_I$ and $\mu_L$, are all equal for the thirty students of
  the background-sound study, on the 0--20 comprehension scale; the
  observed means 12, 10 and 8 estimate them.
- **Conditions:**
  - *Secured by design:* students individually and randomly assigned to
    the sound conditions, ten to each, as the invented study stipulates,
    so a difference among the means reads as an effect of background
    sound among these students; each student read in an individual
    session and was scored once, so the thirty scores come from
    independent units. Assignment does not make the students a random
    sample of a wider population.
  - *Model assumptions:* Normal errors around each group mean with one
    common variance $\sigma^2$, estimated by $MS_W=6.5926$ on 27 df.
  - *Choices and defaults:* all thirty students; a .05 significance
    level fixed in advance; the right tail of $F(2,27)$, because only
    greater separation of the means enlarges F; the classical calibration
    that pools the group variances; all thirty scores observed, so no
    rule for missing outcomes is needed.
- **Check:** the group SDs, 2.7080, 2.4037 and 2.5820, with ten students
  in each group, are similar, the largest 1.1266 times the smallest, and
  the boxplots show no outlying score. Markedly unequal SDs, above all
  with unequal group sizes, would call for Welch's one-way ANOVA
  (Section 5.2), chosen before the analysis. Ten scores per group say
  only a little about the error shape, and independence rests on the
  design, which the scores cannot check.
- **Bound:** $F(2,27)=6.0674$, $p=.0067$ is evidence at the .05 level
  against equal means for these thirty students under the model. It
  does not identify which means differ or by how much (Section 3), and,
  with invented scores, says nothing about real studying.
:::

With equal group sizes $n$, the numerator of F shows directly what the
statistic compares:

$$
F=\frac{n\sum_{j=1}^J(\bar y_j-\bar y)^2/(J-1)}{MS_W}.
$$

Three quantities move it: the separation of the group means, the group
size $n$ and the within-group spread in $MS_W$.
@tbl-ch04-what-moves-f changes one of them at a time, starting from the
thirty invented scores; the second row is the right panel of
@fig-ch04-separation-spread.

\Needspace{11\baselineskip}

| Version of the study | $n$ | Group means | $MS_B$ | $MS_W$ | F | p |
|:--|--:|:--|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| The thirty invented scores | 10 | 12, 10, 8 | 40 | 6.5926 | 6.0674 | .0067 |
| Spread doubled | 10 | 12, 10, 8 | 40 | 26.3704 | 1.5169 | .2375 |
| Separation halved | 10 | 11, 10, 9 | 10 | 6.5926 | 1.5169 | .2375 |
| Group size doubled | 20 | 12, 10, 8 | 80 | 6.5926 | 12.1348 | <.0001 |

: What moves the F statistic: one change at a time to the background-sound study. The last three rows are constructed variations of the invented scores, not further studies; the last has 2 and 57 df, the others 2 and 27. {#tbl-ch04-what-moves-f tbl-colwidths="[34,7,17,11,11,11,9]"}

Doubling every distance from the group mean multiplies $MS_W$ by four,
and halving every mean's distance from the grand mean divides $MS_B$ by
four: each change alone quarters F. F therefore reads separation
relative to spread, never either alone. Doubling the group size with the
same means and SDs leaves every boxplot looking the same, yet doubles
$MS_B$ and so F: more students supply more information about the same
pattern. Section 2.4 shows that a summary of magnitude, eta squared,
barely responds to that third change.

### Two groups, direction and magnitude

ANOVA extends a question about two means to several. For two
independent groups sharing one population variance, Chapter 3,
Section 5.3, used the **equal-variance two-sample t test**, whose SE,
$s_p\sqrt{1/n_1+1/n_0}$, is built from the pooled variance $s_p^2$ of
Chapter 3, Section 2.2. The within-group mean square is that pooled
variance extended to $J$ groups, each group's sample variance $s_j^2$
weighted by its own df:

$$
MS_W=\frac{SS_W}{N-J}
=\frac{\sum_{j=1}^J(n_j-1)s_j^2}{\sum_{j=1}^J(n_j-1)}.
$$

With equal group sizes, $MS_W$ is the plain average of the group
variances, here 7.3333, 5.7778 and 6.6667. With two groups it is
Chapter 3's $s_p^2$, so the classical one-way F test and the
equal-variance t test share one model, one pooled variance and one
residual df, and $F(1,N-2)=t_{N-2}^2$. Chapter 3 labels its two groups 1
and 0; this chapter numbers groups $j=1,\ldots,J$, so its two-group case
uses 1 and 2.

For Silence and Music with lyrics alone, the pooled variance is 7
on 18 df, and $t(18)=3.3806$ and $F(1,18)=11.4286=3.3806^2$ have the
same two-sided $p=.0033$. Squaring removes direction, so the signed
difference, Silence minus Music with lyrics, 4 points, carries it.
This matched fit reads with the [*Justifying the analysis*
box](chapter_03.qmd#ch03-justify-equal-variance) that Chapter 3 gave the
equal-variance t test; only the target changes, to the
Silence-minus-Music-with-lyrics difference for these twenty students,
whose SDs, 2.708 and 2.582, are similar. The two-group refit pools
7.0000 on 18 df rather than the three-group $MS_W=6.5926$ on 27, because
it leaves out the Instrumental group, and it answers a narrower question
than the three-group F: one pairwise comparison rather than the whole
pattern. [Appendix A](#app-ch04-pooled-identity) derives the identity,
and Section 5.2 returns to groups whose spreads may differ.

Magnitude begins on the comprehension scale. The observed
Instrumental-music-minus-Silence difference is $-2$ points and the
Music-with-lyrics-minus-Silence difference is $-4$: two and four
fewer items answered correctly, on average, than in silence. Whether a
difference of this size matters for studying needs a substantive
criterion, not only a p-value. One descriptive summary of the overall
separation is **eta squared**,

$$
\eta^2=\frac{SS_B}{SS_T}=\frac{80}{258}=.3101:
$$

group means account for .3101 of the observed squared variation in these
thirty records. This is a fraction of a sample decomposition, not the
proportion of comprehension caused by background sound. Eta squared and
F answer different questions: in the last row of
@tbl-ch04-what-moves-f, twenty students per group double F while eta
squared barely moves, from .3101 to .2986, because the means account for
about the same share of the variation while the larger study gives
stronger evidence that they differ. A small p-value therefore does not
signal a large difference. Because sample means differ even when model
means are equal, eta squared slightly overstates the share in the model;
omega squared adjusts for that and gives .2525 here
([Appendix B](#app-ch04-effect-sizes)). A standardized mean difference,
explained in [Chapter 3, Section 7.1](chapter_03.qmd#sec-ch03-interpretation),
divides a difference by a stated SD; dividing it by an individual-score
SD gives a different quantity from dividing it by the SE of that
difference.

\Needspace{12\baselineskip}

## Contrasts and Multiple Comparisons {#sec-ch04-contrasts}

### State the comparison through its weights

The omnibus question asks whether all three model means agree. A
**contrast** states a particular comparison as a weighted combination
of means whose weights sum to zero:

$$
C=\sum_{j=1}^Jc_j\mu_j,\qquad \sum_{j=1}^Jc_j=0,
\qquad \widehat C=\sum_{j=1}^Jc_j\bar y_j.
$$

The symbol $C$ here names a contrast, and $\widehat C$ its estimate.
The weights specify both the comparison and its direction.

The study plan declares two questions, each music condition against
Silence: Instrumental music minus Silence and Music with lyrics minus
Silence. A negative estimate means fewer items answered correctly than
in silence. A broader question compares the equal average of the two
music conditions with Silence. In the declared order Silence,
Instrumental music, Music with lyrics, the three comparisons have these
weights:

\Needspace{12\baselineskip}

| Comparison | Weights | Estimate |
|:--|:--|--:|
| Instrumental music minus Silence | $(-1,1,0)$ | $-2$ |
| Music with lyrics minus Silence | $(-1,0,1)$ | $-4$ |
| Equal average of the two music conditions minus Silence | $(-1,1/2,1/2)$ | $-3$ |

: Three contrast meanings in the background-sound study. {#tbl-ch04-weights tbl-colwidths="[55,25,20]"}

Only the first two form the declared family whose intervals Section 3.3
calibrates together. The third comparison gives the two music
conditions equal weight.
It is not a substitute for both separate comparisons when both are
scientifically required. In unequal groups, equal method weights and
weights proportional to student counts answer different questions.
The present groups have equal counts, so the two averaging rules
coincide; [Appendix B](#app-ch04-weighting) develops the distinction.

A grand mean with weights $(1/3,1/3,1/3)$ is a useful linear combination
but not a contrast, because those weights sum to 1. Multiplying every
contrast weight by two doubles the estimate and SE. It preserves a
zero-null t statistic, but changes the quantity being reported. Naming
the comparison in ordinary words prevents a correct calculation from
answering the wrong question.

### Calculate the uncertainty for that comparison

The SE of a contrast extends the two-group SE of Chapter 3,
Section 2.2. A difference between two means is the contrast with
weights $+1$ and $-1$, and Chapter 3's pooled SE can be written with
those weights visible:

$$
s_p\sqrt{\frac{1}{n_1}+\frac{1}{n_0}}
=\sqrt{s_p^2\left(\frac{1^2}{n_1}+\frac{(-1)^2}{n_0}\right)}.
$$

Under the independent common-variance model, each estimated group mean
has variance $\sigma^2/n_j$, and the variance of a weighted sum of
independent means uses the **squared weights**. Opposite signs define a
difference; they do not make independent sources of uncertainty cancel.
Several groups make two changes to Chapter 3's form: the weights $c_j$
can describe any comparison, and $s_p^2$ is replaced by $MS_W$, the
variance pooled over all $J$ groups (Section 2.4). Then

$$
\widehat{SE}(\widehat C)=
\sqrt{MS_W\sum_{j=1}^J\frac{c_j^2}{n_j}}.
$$

For each difference with Silence,

$$
\widehat{SE}=
\sqrt{\frac{178}{27}\left(\frac{1}{10}+\frac{1}{10}\right)}
=1.1483\text{ points}.
$$

Each contrast uses the three-group estimate 6.5926 and its 27 error df,
although it uses only two of the three means: under the common-variance
model all three groups estimate the same $\sigma^2$, so pooling them
uses more information than the two-group refit of Section 2.4, whose
7.0000 on 18 df gives an SE of 1.1832. For the equal-average contrast,
the squared weights $1$, $1/4$ and $1/4$ give $\widehat{SE}=0.9944$.

This smaller SE belongs to a different estimand, an average of two
means compared with the reference. It does not establish that either
separate comparison is more precise than before. The
[NIST contrast explanation](https://www.itl.nist.gov/div898/handbook/prc/section4/prc436.htm)
develops the same weighted-mean variance calculation.

### Families of comparisons and the familywise error rate {#sec-ch04-families}

A study seldom asks only one particular question, and a reader needs to
know how many comparisons were made and when each was chosen. A
**planned comparison** is declared before the results are seen, as this
study's plan declares each music condition against Silence. A **post hoc
comparison** is chosen after the results are seen, often because it
looks large, such as the largest of the three pairwise differences.
[Chapter 3, Section 7.3](chapter_03.qmd#sec-ch03-selection),
showed that a result chosen because it looks large tends to overstate
its target; the same selection problem arises among the several
comparisons of one study.

Each comparison tested at level .05 has a **per-comparison error rate**,
also called the testwise rate, of .05: when its null hypothesis is true,
it rejects wrongly with probability .05. A reader of the whole report,
however, cares whether any of its comparisons is a false rejection. The
**familywise error rate** is the probability of at least one Type I
error (Chapter 3, Section 7.2) among all the comparisons of a family. For $m$ independent
comparisons whose null hypotheses are all true, each tested at .05, it
is $1-(1-.05)^m$, which @fig-ch04-familywise draws against $m$: already
.1426 for three comparisons and .2262 for five.

To hold the familywise rate at .05, **Bonferroni's method** tests each
of the $m$ comparisons at level $.05/m$, or builds each interval with
confidence $1-.05/m$. Its guarantee needs no independence, because the
probability that at least one of several events occurs is at most the
sum of their probabilities:

$$
P(\text{at least one false rejection})
\le\sum_{k=1}^mP(\text{false rejection }k)
=m\cdot\frac{.05}{m}=.05.
$$

[]{#app-ch04-families}The lower line of @fig-ch04-familywise stays at or
below .05 for every $m$. The price is width: each interval is wider and each comparison has
less power, so a family should contain the comparisons that matter
rather than every comparison that could be made. Bonferroni's method
suits any declared set; other methods are calibrated for particular
families and give narrower intervals when their family fits the question
(@tbl-ch04-families) [@tukey1953; @kutner2005].

```{r}
#| label: fig-ch04-familywise
#| fig-cap: "The familywise error rate for m hypothetical independent comparisons whose null hypotheses are all true, each tested at .05 (upper line) or at Bonferroni's .05/m (lower line)."
#| fig-alt: "Two lines over the number of comparisons m, from 1 to 10. The upper line, each comparison tested at .05, rises from .05 at m = 1 through .0975 and .1426, marked at m = 3, and .1855 and .2262, marked at m = 5, to .4013 at m = 10. The lower line, Bonferroni's allocation of .05/m to each comparison, stays just below a dotted reference line at .05 for every m."
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 2.5
#| out-width: 100%
m <- 1:10
each <- 1 - (1 - .05)^m
bonferroni <- 1 - (1 - .05 / m)^m
par(mar = c(4, 4.4, 1, 1))
plot(m, each, type = "b", pch = 16, lwd = 2, ylim = c(0, .45), las = 1,
  xaxt = "n", xlab = "Number of comparisons in the family, m",
  ylab = "Familywise error rate")
axis(1, at = m)
abline(h = .05, col = "grey55", lty = 3)
lines(m, bonferroni, type = "b", pch = 1, lwd = 2, lty = 2,
  col = "#1F5A94")
points(c(3, 5), each[c(3, 5)], pch = 16, cex = 1.7)
text(c(3, 5), each[c(3, 5)], sub("^0", "", num4(each[c(3, 5)])),
  pos = 2, offset = .8, cex = .85)
legend("topleft", c("Each comparison tested at .05",
  "Bonferroni: each tested at .05/m"),
  pch = c(16, 1), lty = 1:2, lwd = 2, col = c("black", "#1F5A94"),
  bty = "n", cex = .85)
```

\Needspace{16\baselineskip}

| Family of comparisons | When it fits | Method that holds the familywise rate |
|:--|:--|:--|
| One comparison | The plan names it in advance as the study's only question | None needed: the ordinary 95% interval, $\widehat C\pm t_{.975}\,\widehat{SE}$ |
| A declared set of $m$ comparisons | The plan names the set before the data are seen | Bonferroni: each comparison at $.05/m$ |
| Each group against one reference | The plan compares every condition with a control or reference condition | Dunnett's method |
| All pairs of groups | Every pairwise difference matters, or a pair is picked after the means are seen | Tukey's method |
| Every contrast, including averages of groups | Any comparison may be formed after the data are seen | Scheffé's method |

: Families of comparisons and the methods that hold the familywise error rate for each. {#tbl-ch04-families tbl-colwidths="[28,42,30]"}

The wider the family, the more comparisons its intervals must cover
together, and the larger the critical value. For one difference between
two sound conditions, on 27 error df, the value for a single planned
comparison is 2.0518 and Scheffé's value for every contrast of the three
means is 2.5900; the declared pair, Tukey's all pairs and Bonferroni's
three pairs fall in between. The family comes from the comparisons for
which coverage is owed, fixed before looking at which interval excludes
zero. An omnibus rejection is not required before a planned comparison,
and it does not by itself protect comparisons chosen afterward.

The study plan declares two comparisons, each music condition against
Silence, so the family is that pair, and Bonferroni gives each interval
97.5% confidence, with .0125 in each tail: the critical value is
$t_{.9875;27}=2.3734$. @tbl-ch04-contrasts gives the two intervals,
$\widehat C\pm2.3734\,\widehat{SE}$.

\Needspace{10\baselineskip}

| Comparison | Estimate | SE | Family lower | Family upper |
|:--|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| Instrumental music minus Silence | $-2$ | 1.1483 | $-4.7253$ | 0.7253 |
| Music with lyrics minus Silence | $-4$ | 1.1483 | $-6.7253$ | $-1.2747$ |

: Bonferroni 95% simultaneous intervals for the two declared comparisons with Silence. {#tbl-ch04-contrasts tbl-colwidths="[36,16,16,16,16]"}

The two estimates share the Silence mean, so they are positively
related: a Silence mean that happens to fall high lowers both
differences together, and their covariance under independent group
means is $\operatorname{Var}(\bar Y_S)=\sigma^2/10$. The union bound
needs no independence, so the joint coverage of at least 95% stands; it
describes repeated use of the whole procedure, not a probability
assigned to the two realized intervals. Dunnett's method, calibrated for
exactly this family of comparisons with one reference, would give
slightly narrower intervals; Bonferroni's arithmetic is the more
transparent. The
[NIST Bonferroni reference](https://www.itl.nist.gov/div898/handbook/prc/section4/prc473.htm)
explains the joint-coverage bound.

[]{#ch04-justify-contrasts}These intervals read with the
[one-way box](#ch04-justify-oneway) of Section 2.3, with three changes.
The target becomes two contrasts in comprehension points, $\mu_I-\mu_S$
and $\mu_L-\mu_S$, rather than the equality of all three means; the
choices add the declared family and Bonferroni's calibration, fixed
before the scores were seen, which only the analysis record can confirm;
and the bound belongs to this declared pair, not to comparisons chosen
after the means were inspected.

The omnibus F and these intervals answer different questions. The F
test says that the three model means are not all equal; the intervals
say which declared differences are established and how large they may
be. Jointly, Music with lyrics minus Silence is negative, between
$-6.7253$ and $-1.2747$ points. The Instrumental-music interval,
$[-4.7253,0.7253]$, includes zero: it is compatible with a small
benefit, no difference or a loss of several points, so it establishes
no equivalence, which would need a declared margin and an analysis
designed for it. These are calculations for invented scores, not a
finding about studying with music.

## Multi-Way (Factorial) ANOVA {#sec-ch04-two-way}

Analysis of variance with two or more crossed factors is **multi-way**,
or **factorial**, ANOVA; this section works the two-way case in full
with the feedback-by-practice study and closes, in Section 4.7, with
three and four factors.

### What interaction means, and why study two factors at once {#sec-ch04-interaction-idea}

Two factors **interact** when the effect of one factor differs across
the levels of the other. Nothing more technical is required to state
the idea. A combination of levels then produces a result that the two
separate comparisons would not have led us to expect.

Here is one invented illustration, outside the chapter's two studies.
Suppose a
short vocabulary preview is given before a reading passage, and that
students are also grouped by whether they began with weak or strong
vocabulary. The preview raises comprehension scores substantially for
the students who began weak, and barely changes them for the students
who began strong. The effect of the preview *depends on* prior
vocabulary: that dependence is the interaction. Describing only an
average preview effect would tell a reader that the preview helps
somewhat, and would conceal that it helps one group a great deal and
the other hardly at all.

Studying two factors together in one crossed design has three
advantages over running two separate one-factor studies.

1. **It is more efficient.** Every student contributes to both factor
   comparisons at once, because the levels of one factor are spread
   across the levels of the other. A crossed design therefore needs
   fewer cases per condition than a series of separate one-factor
   studies aimed at the same comparisons.
2. **It reduces residual variation.** A second factor that influences
   the outcome moves variation out of the error term and into the fit.
   If all 24 students had been analyzed with feedback as the only
   factor, the practice and interaction components, 96 and
   64, would have stayed inside the residual term instead of
   leaving the 60 within-cell error used below. Section 4.4 shows
   what leaving practice out does to these scores.
3. **It makes interaction examinable.** Only a crossed design supports
   the question of whether a comparison changes across the other
   factor's levels. A series of one-factor studies supplies no
   estimate of that change, however carefully each one is run.

In the feedback-by-practice study introduced in Section 1, practice
schedule therefore gives each feedback comparison a context. We can
compare feedback conditions within Massed practice, within Spaced
practice, or after averaging over the two schedules. These are distinct quantities. A **main effect** compares
one factor's levels after averaging across the other factor with
stated weights. A **simple effect** makes the comparison at a
specified level of the other factor. **Interaction** means that a
comparison changes across those levels.

### Main effects and interaction through graphs

In a two-factor design either main effect, the interaction, or any
combination of the three can be present. Six schematic two-by-two
patterns make the whole range visible before we return to the full
three-by-two data. Each line in @fig-ch04-interaction-patterns
represents a feedback level, A or B; the horizontal positions
represent Massed and Spaced practice. These are mean-only drawings,
not additional observed studies, and they carry no significance claim.

```{r}
#| label: fig-ch04-interaction-patterns
#| fig-cap: "Six schematic patterns of cell means, covering the whole range of main-effect and interaction combinations. Lines identify feedback levels A and B; the drawings illustrate averages and changing differences, without significance claims."
#| fig-alt: "Six panels. No effects: A and B coincide as one flat line at 10. One main effect: two separated flat lines at 8 and 12. Two main effects: parallel rising lines. Interaction only: crossing lines with equal marginal means. Interaction qualifies: both lines rise from 8, B more steeply. Interaction reverses: A rises from 8 to 10 while B falls from 16 to 10."
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 4.2
#| out-width: 100%
patterns <- list(
  "No effects" = matrix(c(10, 10, 10, 10), 2, byrow = TRUE),
  "One main effect" = matrix(c(8, 8, 12, 12), 2, byrow = TRUE),
  "Two main effects" = matrix(c(8, 10, 12, 14), 2, byrow = TRUE),
  "Interaction only" = matrix(c(8, 14, 14, 8), 2, byrow = TRUE),
  "Interaction qualifies" = matrix(c(8, 10, 8, 14), 2, byrow = TRUE),
  "Interaction reverses" = matrix(c(8, 10, 16, 10), 2, byrow = TRUE))
par(mfrow = c(2, 3), mar = c(3.6, 3.6, 2.6, .8), mgp = c(2.2, .7, 0))
for (nm in names(patterns)) {
  matplot(1:2, t(patterns[[nm]]), type = "b", pch = c(16, 1),
    lty = c(1, 2), col = c("black", "grey40"),
    ylim = c(6, 19), xlim = c(.85, 2.15), xaxt = "n",
    xlab = "Practice", ylab = "Mean score", main = nm)
  axis(1, at = 1:2, labels = c("Massed", "Spaced"))
  legend("topleft", c("A", "B"), pch = c(16, 1),
    lty = c(1, 2), col = c("black", "grey40"), bty = "n",
    cex = .8, horiz = TRUE)
}
par(mfrow = c(1, 1))
```

Read each pattern by taking differences, not only by recognizing a
shape. Define a schedule difference as Spaced minus Massed and a
difference of differences as B's schedule difference minus A's.

\Needspace{16\baselineskip}

| Pattern | A: Massed, Spaced | B: Massed, Spaced | Schedule differences A, B | Difference of differences |
|:--|:--|:--|:--|--:|
| No effects | 10, 10 | 10, 10 | 0, 0 | 0 |
| One main effect | 8, 8 | 12, 12 | 0, 0 | 0 |
| Two main effects | 8, 10 | 12, 14 | 2, 2 | 0 |
| Interaction only | 8, 14 | 14, 8 | 6, $-6$ | $-12$ |
| Interaction qualifies | 8, 10 | 8, 14 | 2, 6 | 4 |
| Interaction reverses | 8, 10 | 16, 10 | 2, $-6$ | $-8$ |

: Arithmetic behind the six schematic patterns. {#tbl-ch04-patterns tbl-colwidths="[27,17,17,21,18]"}

In the first panel nothing varies: both feedback levels and both
schedules have mean 10, and the two lines coincide. In the second,
B exceeds A by 4 points under either schedule while the schedule
comparison is 0 under either feedback level; there is one main
effect and no interaction. In the third, B still exceeds A by 4
points everywhere, and Spaced now exceeds Massed by 2 points
everywhere: two main effects, again with a zero difference of
differences. Parallel lines express those constant comparisons.

The last three panels have a nonzero difference of differences. In
the crossing panel, both feedback marginal means are 11 and both
practice marginal means are 11 when cells receive equal weight. Both
averaged comparisons are zero despite large conditional differences,
which is why a small main effect need not mean that a factor is
irrelevant at every level of another factor.

In the qualifying panel the schedule comparison is 2 for A and 6 for
B. Both are positive, so the averaged 4-point schedule comparison
points the right way for both feedback levels but describes neither
exactly. The lines need not cross for interaction to be present. In
the reversing panel the schedule comparison is 2 for A and $-6$ for
B, so the averaged comparison of $-2$ points the wrong way for A.
Reporting only the two main effects would then mislead a reader
about every conditional comparison. Examine the interaction first,
and read a main effect as an average whose parts are still visible.

These drawings establish only the numerical patterns: significance
also needs information about variation, sample size and the
reference distribution.

### Cells, marginal means and the full data

Turn to all 24 students of the feedback-by-practice study. Each of the
six cells contains four different students; no person contributes a
score under the other practice schedule. This analysis therefore uses
six separate groups of four, where the background-sound analysis used
three groups of ten.

Write $\bar y_{jk}$ for a cell mean, with $j=1,2,3$ indexing feedback
and $k=1,2$ indexing practice. A dot replaces an index that has been
averaged over: $\bar y_{j\cdot}$ averages a feedback level over
practice, and $\bar y_{\cdot k}$ averages a practice level over
feedback. An **effect** in this layout is a marginal mean's departure
from the grand mean, 10. @tbl-ch04-cell-means gives the cell means, the
equally weighted marginal means and the effects.

\Needspace{15\baselineskip}

| Feedback | Massed | Spaced | Feedback mean | Feedback effect |
|:--|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| Rereading | 6 | 6 | 6 | $-4$ |
| Answer feedback | 8 | 12 | 10 | 0 |
| Explanatory feedback | 10 | 18 | 14 | 4 |
| Practice mean | 8 | 12 | Grand mean 10 | |
| Practice effect | $-2$ | 2 | | |

: Cell means, equally weighted marginal means and effects for the complete invented study. {#tbl-ch04-cell-means tbl-colwidths="[27,13,13,26,21]"}

Each marginal mean averages its cell means with equal weights; with four
students in every cell it is also the mean of that condition's students.
The feedback effects, $-4$, 0 and 4, and the practice effects, $-2$ and
2, each sum to zero. The practice comparison, Spaced minus Massed,
averages 4 points over the three feedback conditions, but its
components, the schedule differences within the rows, are 0,
4 and 8. A four-point main effect is therefore a meaningful
stated average that describes none of the conditional comparisons except
Answer feedback's.

```{r}
#| label: fig-ch04-cell-means
#| fig-cap: "Quiz cell means across practice schedules in the full 3 × 2 example. Each line joins means of different students; the schedule differences are 0, 4 and 8 points."
#| fig-alt: "Rereading stays at 6 from Massed to Spaced practice. Answer feedback rises from 8 to 12. Explanatory feedback rises from 10 to 18. The nonparallel lines show that the schedule comparison changes across feedback conditions."
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 3.8
#| out-width: 100%
par(mar = c(4, 4, 1, 1), cex = .9)
with(feedback_data,
  interaction.plot(practice, feedback, score, type = "b",
    pch = c(16, 1, 17), lty = 1:3,
    col = c("#202020", "#2B6CA3", "#9B4922"),
    xlab = "Practice schedule", ylab = "Mean quiz score",
    trace.label = "Feedback", ylim = c(0, 20)))
```

The connected lines in @fig-ch04-cell-means organize cell means. They
do not show individual students moving from one condition to another.
The nonparallel pattern describes interaction in the observed means;
the full model supplies the uncertainty calculation for an inferential
claim.

### Additivity and the full model {#sec-ch04-full-model}

If feedback and practice combined additively, every cell mean would be
the grand mean plus its feedback effect plus its practice effect, and
the schedule difference would be the same in every row.
@tbl-ch04-interaction-departures sets these **additive predictions**
beside the observed cell means. The difference between an observed cell
mean and its additive prediction is an **interaction departure**.

\Needspace{12\baselineskip}

| Cell | Observed mean | Additive prediction | Interaction departure |
|:--|--:|--:|--:|
| Rereading, Massed | 6 | 4 | 2 |
| Rereading, Spaced | 6 | 8 | $-2$ |
| Answer feedback, Massed | 8 | 8 | 0 |
| Answer feedback, Spaced | 12 | 12 | 0 |
| Explanatory feedback, Massed | 10 | 12 | $-2$ |
| Explanatory feedback, Spaced | 18 | 16 | 2 |

: Observed cell means, additive predictions from the grand mean and both effects, and interaction departures. {#tbl-ch04-interaction-departures tbl-colwidths="[37,19,22,22]"}

Answer feedback's two cells sit exactly on their predictions, but the
other four do not: Rereading gains less from spacing than the average,
and Explanatory feedback more, by 2 points in each cell. Agreement in
one row does not make the whole layout additive.

The full mean model includes such departures:

$$
Y_{ijk}=\mu+\alpha_j+\beta_k+(\alpha\beta)_{jk}
        +\varepsilon_{ijk}.
$$

Here $i=1,\ldots,4$ identifies a student within a cell, $j=1,2,3$
identifies feedback and $k=1,2$ identifies practice. The grand model
mean is $\mu$; $\alpha_j$ and $\beta_k$ are the factor effects;
$(\alpha\beta)_{jk}$ is the interaction departure; and
$\varepsilon_{ijk}$ is the individual error around the cell mean.
These indexed effects are distinct from the unindexed error
probabilities $\alpha$ and $\beta$ used in hypothesis testing.

In the balanced decomposition, main effects sum to zero, and
interaction departures sum to zero along each row and each column, so
they carry only the pattern left after the two main effects. With two
columns, a row's second departure is the negative of its first, and the
three first-column departures, 2, 0 and $-2$, sum to zero, so only two
of them are free. Thus the interaction has $(3-1)(2-1)=2$ df. It
describes a two-dimensional pattern, rather than one particular
four-cell difference.

[]{#app-ch04-two-way-arithmetic}Each score's distance from the grand
mean now splits into four parts, a feedback effect, a practice effect,
an interaction departure and the student's residual. Squaring the parts
and adding over all 24 students gives, in this balanced layout as in
Section 2.2, four sums of squares with matching df:

$$
SS_T=SS_A+SS_B+SS_{AB}+SS_E,\qquad
df_T=df_A+df_B+df_{AB}+df_E.
$$

In this two-way table A denotes feedback and B practice, so $SS_B$ now
means the practice component, not the between-group component of the
one-way table, and $SS_E$ is the within-cell error:

$$
\begin{aligned}
SS_A&=2n\sum_j(\bar y_{j\cdot}-\bar y)^2=256,\\
SS_B&=3n\sum_k(\bar y_{\cdot k}-\bar y)^2=96,\\
SS_{AB}&=n\sum_j\sum_k
 (\bar y_{jk}-\bar y_{j\cdot}-\bar y_{\cdot k}+\bar y)^2
 =64,\\
SS_E&=\sum_j\sum_k\sum_i(y_{ijk}-\bar y_{jk})^2=60.
\end{aligned}
$$

Each component counts its effects or departures once for every student
who shares them. The partition reads
$476=256+96+64+60$ on $23=2+1+2+18$ df: each of
the six cells uses one mean, so the error has $24-6=18$ df, and the fit
part is $256+96+64=416$ on five df.

\Needspace{14\baselineskip}

| Source | SS | df | MS | F | p |
|:--|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| Feedback (A) | 256 | 2 | 128.0000 | 38.4 | <.0001 |
| Practice (B) | 96 | 1 | 96.0000 | 28.8 | <.0001 |
| A × B | 64 | 2 | 32.0000 | 9.6 | .0015 |
| Error | 60 | 18 | 3.3333 | | |
| Total | 476 | 23 | | | |

: Full two-way ANOVA using all 24 students. {#tbl-ch04-two-way-anova}

Read this table as in [Section 2.3](#sec-ch04-anova-table): the three
source rows are the fit, the error row the residual and the total the
data, and the sums of squares and df add across the rows. Read the
interaction row first, because it decides how the two main-effect rows
can be read.

The error row of @tbl-ch04-two-way-anova holds only the variation of
students around their own cell means. @fig-ch04-ignore-practice shows
what happens to that row if practice is left out of the model, so that
each feedback condition becomes one group of eight students. This is
not an analysis the design calls for; it shows what the second factor
removes from the error term.

```{r}
#| label: fig-ch04-ignore-practice
#| fig-cap: "The 24 feedback-by-practice scores analysed two ways. Left: practice is left out, so each feedback condition is one group of eight; filled circles mark Massed and triangles Spaced students. Right: the six cells of the full model, with a bar at each cell mean. Leaving practice out moves the practice and interaction variation into the within-group term."
#| fig-alt: "Two panels on a 0 to 20 quiz-score axis. Left: three boxplots of eight scores each. Rereading runs from 4 to 8, its Massed and Spaced scores identical; Answer feedback runs from 6 to 14; Explanatory feedback runs from 8 to 20, its Massed scores 8 to 12 and Spaced scores 16 to 20 forming two clusters. Beneath it: within-group MS 10.4762 on 21 df, feedback F(2, 21) = 12.2182. Right: the same scores in six cells of four, each spanning four points around its cell mean: 6 and 6 for Rereading, 8 and 12 for Answer feedback, 10 and 18 for Explanatory feedback, Massed then Spaced. Beneath it: within-cell MS 3.3333 on 18 df, feedback F(2, 18) = 38.4."
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 3.9
#| out-width: 100%
short <- c("Rereading", "Answer", "Explanatory")
symbol <- ifelse(feedback_data$practice == "Massed", 16, 2)
par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(5.4, 4.2, 2.4, .8), cex.main = .95)
boxplot(score ~ feedback, data = feedback_data, ylim = c(0, 20), las = 1,
  names = short, col = "grey92", border = "grey40", cex.axis = .85,
  xlab = "", ylab = "Quiz score (0-20)",
  main = "Practice ignored: 3 groups of 8")
points(as.integer(feedback_data$feedback) +
    ifelse(feedback_data$practice == "Massed", -.13, .13),
  feedback_data$score, pch = symbol, cex = .8)
legend("topleft", c("Massed", "Spaced"), pch = c(16, 2), bty = "n",
  cex = .8)
mtext("Within-group MS 10.4762 on 21 df", side = 1, line = 2.6, cex = .8)
mtext("Feedback F(2, 21) = 12.2182", side = 1, line = 3.6, cex = .8)
cell <- interaction(feedback_data$practice, feedback_data$feedback)
cell_mean <- tapply(feedback_data$score, cell, mean)
plot(as.integer(cell), feedback_data$score, pch = symbol, cex = .8,
  xlim = c(.5, 6.5), ylim = c(0, 20), xaxt = "n", las = 1, xlab = "",
  ylab = "Quiz score (0-20)", main = "Full model: 6 cells of 4")
segments(1:6 - .3, cell_mean, 1:6 + .3, cell_mean, lwd = 2.5,
  col = "#9B4922")
axis(1, at = 1:6, labels = rep(c("M", "S"), 3), cex.axis = .8, padj = -.8)
axis(1, at = c(1.5, 3.5, 5.5), labels = short, tick = FALSE, line = .6,
  cex.axis = .85)
mtext("Within-cell MS 3.3333 on 18 df", side = 1, line = 3, cex = .8)
mtext("Feedback F(2, 18) = 38.4", side = 1, line = 4, cex = .8)
```

\Needspace{12\baselineskip}

| Analysis of the 24 scores | The within-group term holds | Error SS | Error df | Error MS | Feedback F | p |
|:--|:--|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| Feedback only, practice left out | Within-cell error 60, practice 96 and interaction 64 | 220 | 21 | 10.4762 | 12.2182 | .0003 |
| Full two-way model | Within-cell error 60 only | 60 | 18 | 3.3333 | 38.4000 | <.0001 |

: What leaving practice out does to the error term. {#tbl-ch04-ignore-practice tbl-colwidths="[23,27,11,8,10,13,8]"}

Leaving practice out changes neither the feedback means, 6,
10 and 14, nor the feedback sum of squares, 256; it
changes the error term. The practice and interaction components stay
inside the within-group variation, which becomes
$220=60+96+64$ on 21 df, so the within-group mean square,
10.4762, is more than three times the full model's 3.3333 and the
feedback F falls from 38.4000 to 12.2182. The left panel shows where
the extra variation comes from: each group mixes two schedules, so the
Explanatory group splits into two clusters eight points apart and its
SD, 4.5981, is 2.7203 times Rereading's 1.6903, whose two schedules do
not differ. One pooled variance would misdescribe all three groups. A
factor that influences the outcome belongs in the model, which is the
second advantage of a crossed design in Section 4.1.

Every displayed F divides its source mean square by the same
$MS_E=60/18=10/3$. The corresponding null hypotheses address
different features of the model:

\Needspace{12\baselineskip}

| Source | Null hypothesis | Comparison represented |
|:--|:--|:--|
| Feedback | $\mu_{R\cdot}=\mu_{A\cdot}=\mu_{E\cdot}$ | Equal feedback means, each averaging the two schedules equally |
| Practice | $\mu_{\cdot M}=\mu_{\cdot S}$ | Equal schedule means, each averaging the three feedback levels equally |
| Interaction | $(\alpha\beta)_{jk}=0$ for every cell | Each feedback comparison is constant across schedules, equivalently each schedule difference is the same across feedback levels |

: Three null hypotheses with their averaging rules. {#tbl-ch04-factorial-nulls tbl-colwidths="[17,37,46]"}

Independent common-variance Normal errors supply the classical F
references. Under these conditions, the interaction result
$F(2,18)=9.6$, $p=.0015$ gives evidence against an additive
pattern. Both main effects also have small p-values, but their
meanings remain averaged comparisons. Reading them as “each factor
works equally well everywhere” would discard the interaction.

The clean component decomposition uses the balanced layout. With
unequal cell counts, the averaging target and the model comparison
need more care; different software sums of squares can address
different hypotheses. The [weighting reference](#app-ch04-weighting)
explains the first distinction without changing these data.

[]{#ch04-justify-factorial}

::: {.callout-tip title="Justifying the analysis"}
- **Target:** the six cell means $\mu_{jk}$ of the feedback-by-practice
  layout for the 24 students, in quiz points. The three F tests ask
  whether the equally weighted feedback means are equal, whether the two
  equally weighted practice means are equal, and whether every
  interaction departure is zero.
- **Conditions:**
  - *Secured by design:* students individually and randomly assigned to
    the six cells, four different students in each, each scored once; no
    student contributes a score under both schedules.
  - *Model assumptions:* Normal errors with one common variance in every
    cell, estimated by $MS_E=3.3333$ on 18 df. The model includes the interaction, so it does not assume additivity. A main effect remains a defined average over the other factor's levels; reading it as the effect at every level would assume additivity.
  - *Choices and defaults:* the full model with interaction; equal cell
    weights for the marginal means; a .05 level fixed in advance. With four
    students in every cell, every sums-of-squares convention gives the
    same table.
- **Check:** every cell has residuals $-2$, $-1$, 1 and 2, so the six
  spreads agree by construction; residuals fanning out as the fitted
  mean grows would question the common variance. Four scores per cell say little about shape. The interaction
  row, $F(2,18)=9.6$, $p=.0015$, together with the cell-mean plot,
  shows that additivity fails for these scores.
- **Bound:** under the model, the evidence is against an additive
  pattern. The main effects, $F(2,18)=38.4$ and $F(1,18)=28.8$,
  both $p<.0001$, describe equally weighted averages; the schedule
  differences within the three feedback conditions, 0, 4 and
  8 points, show what those averages conceal. The scores are
  invented, so the result describes a calculation, not an educational
  finding.
:::

### Simple effects and a selected interaction contrast

The Answer-feedback schedule comparison, Spaced minus Massed, is a
**simple effect**: $12-8=4$ points. Under the full model its SE is
$\sqrt{(10/3)(1/4+1/4)}=1.291$, and with 18 error df a pointwise 95%
interval is $[1.2877,6.7123]$. This interval covers the one stated
simple comparison; it is not protected for every simple effect that a
reader might inspect after seeing the graph. The two means come from
different students, so this is an independent-cell calculation, not a
paired one.

Now suppose a reader selects the Answer-versus-Rereading change in the
schedule comparison after inspecting the pattern. In model means the
target is

$$
C=(\mu_{A,S}-\mu_{A,M})-(\mu_{R,S}-\mu_{R,M}),
$$

one **difference of differences**, estimated as $(12-8)-(6-6)=4$.
Its four cell means come from different students and carry weights 1,
$-1$, $-1$ and 1, so squaring the weights gives
$\widehat{SE}(\widehat C)=\sqrt{(10/3)(1/4+1/4+1/4+1/4)}=1.8257$.
Because the contrast was chosen after the graph was seen, its interval
must cover every interaction contrast that could have been chosen:
Scheffé's family for **all contrasts in the two-dimensional interaction
space**, with multiplier $\sqrt{2F_{.95;2,18}}=2.6663$, gives
$4\pm2.6663(1.8257)\approx[-0.868,8.868]$.

This interval reads with [the contrast sentences of
Section 3.3](#ch04-justify-contrasts), with these changes: the design
and check are those of the [factorial box](#ch04-justify-factorial) in
Section 4.4; the target is a difference of differences among four cell
means; the error estimate is the full model's $MS_E=3.3333$ on 18 df;
and the family is Scheffé's, because the comparison was selected after
inspection.

The interval includes zero even though the omnibus interaction p-value
is .0015. There is no contradiction. The joint test assesses the entire
two-dimensional departure from additivity; the selected contrast
concerns one direction, with protection for choosing among all
interaction contrasts. Evidence that some interaction direction is
nonzero does not establish every selected direction. Had the plan named
this one contrast before the scores were seen, the pointwise interval
$[0.1643,7.8357]$ would be warranted, and it excludes zero; choosing it
now because it excludes zero would discard the protection that the
selection requires. Here the history of the comparison decides the
conclusion.

The protected space is specific. The simple Answer schedule effect
contains a practice main-effect component as well as an interaction
component, so it lies outside this interaction-only family, and all
contrasts among the six cell means would form a larger,
five-dimensional space with a larger multiplier. A claim covering those
comparisons would need its own family.

### Give a connected interpretation

The observed schedule differences are 0, 4 and 8
quiz points for Rereading, Answer feedback and Explanatory feedback.
The full-model interaction test gives $F(2,18)=9.6$, $p=.0015$
under the stated conditions. The selected Answer-versus-Rereading
change in schedule difference is 4 points, with a 95% Scheffé
interval $[-0.868,8.868]$ over all interaction contrasts. The
overall result does not establish that particular selected comparison.

Feedback and practice marginal means summarize explicit equal
weights. The cell means show what those averages can conceal. The
one-way conclusions of Sections 2 and 3 concern the background-sound
study, whereas this factorial conclusion uses all 24 students of the
feedback-by-practice study and 18 error df.
These are analyses of invented data, not empirical evidence that a
teaching method succeeds in a population of students.

### Three and four factors {#sec-ch04-multiway}

Suppose a larger version of the feedback-by-practice study added a
third factor, quiz timing: students take the quiz either right after
their final practice or one week later. Crossing timing with the six
feedback-by-practice cells gives twelve cells, a three-way layout, with
four different students in each cell. The extension is hypothetical,
and @fig-ch04-three-way draws cell means only: it shows a pattern, not
data, and carries no significance claim.

```{r}
#| label: fig-ch04-three-way
#| fig-cap: "A hypothetical three-way pattern, drawn as cell means only. Each panel is the feedback-by-practice plot for one quiz timing. Right after practice the lines are parallel, so Answer's schedule difference minus Rereading's is 0; one week later they fan out, and the same difference of differences is 4. That change across timing is a three-way interaction."
#| fig-alt: "Two panels of hypothetical cell means on a 0 to 20 quiz-score axis, with practice schedule on the horizontal axis and one line per feedback condition. Left panel, quiz right after practice: Rereading rises from 8 to 10, Answer feedback from 10 to 12 and Explanatory feedback from 12 to 14, three parallel lines; beneath it, Spaced minus Massed: 2, 2 and 2. Right panel, quiz one week later: Rereading stays at 6, Answer feedback rises from 7 to 11 and Explanatory feedback from 8 to 16, so the lines fan out; beneath it, Spaced minus Massed: 0, 4 and 8."
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 3.2
#| out-width: 100%
three_way <- list(
  "Quiz right after practice" = rbind(Rereading = c(8, 10),
    Answer = c(10, 12), Explanatory = c(12, 14)),
  "Quiz one week later" = rbind(Rereading = c(6, 6),
    Answer = c(7, 11), Explanatory = c(8, 16)))
note <- c("Spaced minus Massed: 2, 2 and 2",
  "Spaced minus Massed: 0, 4 and 8")
line_col <- c("#202020", "#2B6CA3", "#9B4922")
par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(5.2, 4.2, 2.4, .8), cex.main = .95)
for (p in 1:2) {
  matplot(1:2, t(three_way[[p]]), type = "b", pch = c(16, 1, 17),
    lty = 1:3, col = line_col, ylim = c(0, 20), xlim = c(.8, 2.2),
    xaxt = "n", las = 1, xlab = "",
    ylab = "Mean quiz score (hypothetical)", main = names(three_way)[p])
  axis(1, at = 1:2, labels = c("Massed", "Spaced"))
  mtext(note[p], side = 1, line = 2.6, cex = .8)
  if (p == 1) legend("bottomright", c("Rereading", "Answer", "Explanatory"),
    pch = c(16, 1, 17), lty = 1:3, col = line_col, bty = "n", cex = .8)
}
par(mfrow = c(1, 1))
```

Read each panel as @fig-ch04-cell-means was read. Right after practice
the three lines are parallel: spacing adds 2 points under every kind of
feedback, so Answer's schedule difference minus Rereading's is
$2-2=0$, and this panel shows no two-way interaction. One week later
the lines fan out: spacing adds 0, 4 and 8 points, and the same
difference of differences is $4-0=4$. The feedback-by-practice
interaction therefore differs between the two timings, and that change
is a **three-way interaction**: a two-way pattern that changes across
the levels of a third factor. One three-way contrast is the change in
the difference of differences, $4-0=4$ points, a difference of
differences of differences.

A fourth factor carries the idea one level further. Suppose the study
also crossed reading on paper or on screen with the twelve cells, each
student reading the practice material in one medium, again with four
different students in each of the 24 cells. A **four-way interaction**
would mean that the three-way pattern itself differs between the two
media: for example, that the pattern of @fig-ch04-three-way, parallel
lines right after practice and lines fanning out by feedback a week
later, holds for students who read on paper, while for students who
read on screen the lines stay parallel at both timings.
@tbl-ch04-multiway counts what each added factor brings when every
cell keeps four different students.

Each added two-level factor doubles the cells, so four students per
cell means 24, then 48, then 96 students. The effects grow faster than
the factors: a design with $k$ factors has $k$ main effects and one
interaction for every pair, triple and larger set of factors, $2^k-1$
sources in all, so a three-factor table has seven rows of effects and a
four-factor table fifteen.

Read such a table from the highest-order interaction down. Section 4.4
read the interaction row before the main effects, because a main
effect averages over a pattern that the interaction says is changing.
One level up the rule is the same: when a three-way interaction is
present, each two-way interaction is an average over the levels of the
third factor. Averaged over the two timings of @fig-ch04-three-way,
