Answer's schedule difference minus Rereading's is 2 points, which
describes neither panel. Report the two-way patterns within each level
of the third factor instead, and read a lower-order row alone only when
the design and the evidence make the higher-order interactions
negligible [@kutner2005].

\Needspace{14\baselineskip}

| Design | 3 × 2 | 3 × 2 × 2 | 3 × 2 × 2 × 2 |
|:--|--:|--:|--:|
| Cells | 6 | 12 | 24 |
| Students, four per cell | 24 | 48 | 96 |
| Main effects, one per factor, $k$ | 2 | 3 | 4 |
| Two-way interactions | 1 | 3 | 6 |
| Three-way interactions | 0 | 1 | 4 |
| Four-way interactions | 0 | 0 | 1 |
| Sources of effects, $2^k-1$ | 3 | 7 | 15 |
| Error df, students minus cells | 18 | 36 | 72 |

: Cells, students, effects and error df as quiz timing and then reading medium are added to the feedback-by-practice design, four students per cell. {#tbl-ch04-multiway tbl-colwidths="[40,20,20,20]"}

Added factors have costs. A three-way contrast combines eight cell
means where a difference of differences combines four, so with the same
students per cell and the same error variance its SE is $\sqrt2$, about
1.4, times as large, and matching the precision of a difference of
differences takes twice as many students per cell. The seven F tests of
a three-factor table, each at .05, also form a family in the sense of
[Section 3.3](#sec-ch04-families): for seven independent tests whose
null hypotheses are all true, the chance of at least one false
rejection is .3017, where the upper line of @fig-ch04-familywise stands
at $m=7$, and the fifteen tests of a four-factor table raise it
further. More cells also make unequal or empty cells more likely:
unequal counts make each marginal mean depend on its weights
([Appendix B.1](#app-ch04-weighting)), and an empty cell leaves some
interactions without an estimate.

A study with several factors therefore declares in advance the few
comparisons it was built for, such as whether the spacing benefit under
Answer feedback grows between the two timings, and reads the other rows
and cells as description. Twelve cells allow 66 pairwise comparisons and
many more contrasts, so a comparison found by searching them needs a
family that covers the search, as Section 3.3 showed for three groups.

## Checking the Conditions {#sec-ch04-conditions}

### What the design and the data can show {#sec-ch04-deeper-checks}

Sections 2--4 stated each condition where a procedure first relied on
it, and each *Justifying the analysis* box recorded what the data could
check. @tbl-ch04-conditions gathers the conditions of the chapter's
analyses, what the design or the data can show about each, and the
response when one fails.

A sequence of Normality or variance tests should not become an automatic
permission rule: such tests have least power in the small samples where
the choice matters most. A condition is judged from the design, subject
knowledge and displays such as @fig-ch04-residuals together
[@kutner2005].

\Needspace{20\baselineskip}

| Condition | What the design or the data can show | Response if it fails |
|:--|:--|:--|
| Independent observations | Only the design record: individual assignment, individual sessions, one score per student. No display of the scores can establish it | An analysis that represents the dependence: comparisons within blocks, as in Chapter 3's paired schools (Section 2.3), or models for classes and repeated measurements. Treating dependent rows as independent misstates every SE; positive clustering makes it too small, by about the square root of the design effect of Chapter 2, Section 4.4 |
| Roughly Normal errors around the group or cell means | A residual display and a Normal quantile plot of the residuals, not of the pooled scores; small groups reveal only pronounced departures | With moderate skew and larger groups the F reference remains a reasonable approximation; with small groups and strong skew or a dominating value, disclose the weaker approximation and examine the influential scores |
| One common variance | The group or cell SDs beside the group sizes; a fan in the residuals as the fitted mean grows | Welch's one-way ANOVA, chosen before the analysis (Section 5.2); for a contrast, an SE built from its groups' own variances, which for a pair is Chapter 3's Welch t |
| Additivity, when a main effect is read as the effect at every level | The interaction row and the cell-mean plot | Report cell means and simple effects, and read each main effect as a stated average (Section 4) |

: Conditions of the chapter's analyses, what can show whether each holds, and the response if it fails. {#tbl-ch04-conditions tbl-colwidths="[22,38,40]"}

```{r}
#| label: fig-ch04-residuals
#| fig-cap: "Residuals of the one-way fit to the background-sound scores. Left: each student's residual, the score minus the group mean, by condition, jittered sideways so that equal values stay visible. Right: the thirty residuals against Normal quantiles, with a reference line."
#| fig-alt: "Left panel: three vertical strips of ten points, for Silence, Instrumental music and Music with lyrics, each spread from -4 to 4 around a dashed line at zero, with similar spread in every group. Right panel: a Normal quantile plot of the thirty residuals; the points rise in whole-number steps and follow a dashed reference line, the residuals of -4 and of 4 at the two ends sitting flatter than the line, and no point is far from it."
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 3.3
#| out-width: 100%
res <- residuals(one_way)
par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(4, 4.2, 2.2, .8), cex.main = .95)
set.seed(12345)
stripchart(res ~ sound_data$sound, vertical = TRUE, method = "jitter",
  jitter = .12, pch = 16, cex = .8, las = 1, cex.axis = .85,
  group.names = c("Silence", "Instrumental", "Lyrics"),
  ylab = "Residual (score minus group mean)",
  main = "Residuals by condition")
abline(h = 0, lty = 2)
qqnorm(res, pch = 16, cex = .8, las = 1, main = "Normal quantile plot",
  xlab = "Normal quantile", ylab = "Residual")
qqline(res, lty = 2)
par(mfrow = c(1, 1))
```

For the background-sound study the residuals spread similarly around
zero in all three groups, each from $-4$ to 4, and in the quantile plot
they follow the line, with no outlying value; the residuals of $-4$ and
4 at the two ends sit a little flatter than a Normal tail. Thirty
residuals can
show only pronounced departures, so the display is consistent with the
model rather than proof of it, and independence still rests on the
design. The factorial scores were built with residuals $-2$, $-1$, 1 and
2 in every cell, a teaching construction that no display could treat as
evidence.

Missing outcomes raise a further question that neither the model nor a
display answers. A report compares assigned and analysed counts and
explains known reasons for losses, because missing outcomes can change
who contributes to a comparison and can require assumptions beyond the
ANOVA model. Neither invented dataset has missing scores: all 30
background-sound scores and all 24 feedback-by-practice scores are
observed. Keep three claims distinct in every report: the observed means
and sums of squares describe these records; intervals and tests express
uncertainty under a stated model; and causal or population
interpretations need support from allocation, participation, measurement
and the intended scope.

### When spreads differ: Welch's one-way ANOVA {#sec-ch04-welch}

When a common variance is doubtful, **Welch's one-way ANOVA** is the
counterpart of Welch's unequal-variance t test in Chapter 3,
Section 5.4. It keeps each group's own variance instead of pooling them
into $MS_W$, weights each group mean by the precision implied by its own
variance and size, $n_j/s_j^2$, and uses an approximate F reference
whose denominator df are estimated from the group variances
[@welch1951]; with two groups its F is the square of Welch's t.
[]{#ch04-justify-welch}It reads with the
[one-way box](#ch04-justify-oneway) of Section 2.3, with two changes:
the model assumption of one common variance is dropped, so each group
mean needs only a near-Normal sampling distribution, and the calibration
changes with it. For the background-sound study it gives
$F(2,17.9561)=5.5144$, $p=.0136$, beside the classical
$F(2,27)=6.0674$, $p=.0067$: with similar spreads and equal group sizes
the two calibrations lead to the same conclusion at .05, although
Welch's p is about twice as large. Its F is slightly smaller, and its
denominator df fall from 27 to 17.9561 because each weight rests on a
variance estimated from its own ten scores. Welch's
method has the scope of one factor: clustering still needs an analysis
that represents the design, and crossed factors with unequal cell
spreads take each stated contrast's SE from the cells' own variances.

The classical F test applies one pooled variance to every group mean.
Chapter 3, Section 5.4, showed for two groups that a pooled variance
misstates the variance of a small group's mean when spreads differ.
@tbl-ch04-welch-consequence shows what this does with three groups: each
row simulates 50,000 studies of three Normal groups with equal means and
the stated SDs, so every rejection at level .05 rejects a true null.

```{r}
#| label: ch04-welch-sim
#| include: false
# Recomputes the rates printed in tbl-ch04-welch-consequence and stops the
# render if any printed value no longer matches.
simulate_design <- function(n, s, B = 50000) {
  set.seed(12345)
  J <- length(n); N <- sum(n)
  means <- vars <- matrix(NA, nrow = B, ncol = J)
  for (j in 1:J) {
    x <- matrix(rnorm(B * n[j], mean = 0, sd = s[j]), nrow = n[j])
    means[, j] <- colMeans(x)
    vars[, j] <- apply(x, 2, var)
  }
  grand <- drop(means %*% n) / N
  MS_B <- drop((means - grand)^2 %*% n) / (J - 1)
  MS_W <- drop(vars %*% (n - 1)) / (N - J)
  w <- sweep(1 / vars, 2, n, "*")
  W <- rowSums(w)
  weighted_mean <- rowSums(w * means) / W
  S <- drop((1 - w / W)^2 %*% (1 / (n - 1)))
  F_welch <- rowSums(w * (means - weighted_mean)^2) / (J - 1) /
    (1 + 2 * (J - 2) / (J^2 - 1) * S)
  nu <- (J^2 - 1) / (3 * S)
  c(classical = mean(MS_B / MS_W > qf(.95, df1 = J - 1, df2 = N - J)),
    welch = mean(F_welch > qf(.95, df1 = J - 1, df2 = nu)))
}
welch_rates <- rbind(simulate_design(c(10, 20, 40), c(8, 4, 4)),
  simulate_design(c(10, 20, 40), c(4, 4, 8)),
  simulate_design(c(20, 20, 20), c(8, 4, 4)))
stopifnot(sprintf("%.4f", welch_rates) ==
  c("0.1572", "0.0126", "0.0610", "0.0511", "0.0499", "0.0502"),
  sprintf("%.4f", 1504 / 67) == "22.4478",
  sprintf("%.4f", 1504 / 67 / 10) == "2.2448")
```

\Needspace{14\baselineskip}

| Group sizes | Population SDs | Classical F | Welch's one-way ANOVA |
|:--|:--|--:|--:|
| 10, 20 and 40 | 8, 4 and 4: the smallest group varies most | .1572 | .0511 |
| 10, 20 and 40 | 4, 4 and 8: the largest group varies most | .0126 | .0499 |
| 20, 20 and 20 | 8, 4 and 4 | .0610 | .0502 |

: Rejection rates of a true null of equal means at nominal level .05, from 50,000 simulated studies per design. {#tbl-ch04-welch-consequence tbl-colwidths="[18,42,20,20]"}

When the smallest group varies most, the variance that pooling targets,
22.4478, gives that group's mean a variance of 2.2448 instead of the
6.4000 its own SD implies, and the classical F rejects the true null in
.1572 of the studies, more than three times the nominal .05; when the
largest group varies most it rejects in only .0126, and with equal group
sizes it rises only to .0610. Welch's one-way ANOVA stays near .05 in all
three designs, which is why unequal group sizes with spreads that may
differ call for it.

As in Chapter 3, choose between the common-variance and Welch
calibrations before the analysis, from the design and subject knowledge,
rather than from a preliminary variance test or from whichever p-value
is smaller [@delacre2017; @delacre2019]. Many statistical programs
report Welch's t by default for two groups; that default is Chapter 3's
last t procedure, not the equal-variance test whose square equals the
classical F of Section 2.4. Chapter 6 runs the Welch alternative beside
the common-variance calculation.

## Reading Bridge {#sec-ch04-bridge}

Comparing several means extends the estimate-and-SE reasoning of
Chapter 3. ANOVA separates sources of variation to ask an omnibus
question; a contrast states a narrower question and its uncertainty.
Main effects average across factor levels, while cell means and
simple effects show the conditional pattern, and a third factor can
change a two-way pattern itself. A joint interaction test and one
selected interaction contrast can therefore lead to different,
compatible conclusions.

The same group-mean model can be written using indicator variables,
as Chapter 6 does in R. A measured baseline can also enter an adjusted
model, called analysis of covariance (ANCOVA), which Chapter 9,
Section 2, develops as regression after Chapters 7--8 develop the
regression mathematics, several controls and standardized
predictions. Baseline adjustment accounts for a measured
source of score variation and compares fitted outcomes at a stated common
baseline value, or averages them over the same stated baseline distribution.
The groups need adequate overlap in those baseline values, often called
common support, for those comparisons to be informed by observations.
Adjustment is not a general cure for confounding or missing outcomes.

Blocking organizes comparisons within allocation groups, as in
Chapter 3's paired schools (Section 2.3). Repeated measurements and
classroom clustering change the covariance structure and the
relevant error term. The shape of a data table cannot settle these
design questions. Chapters 5--6 now make the statistical foundations
executable while keeping the question, records and interpretation
beside each calculation.

### Key terms {.unnumbered}

Use this reference to revisit the concepts principally explained here.
The Part One Concept Reference collects earlier terms, including
estimand, SE and confidence interval.

```{=latex}
\small
```

| Term and common alternatives | Meaning |
|:--|:--|
| Factor (grouping factor) | In ANOVA, a categorical variable defining groups or conditions; its categories are levels. This meaning differs from a latent factor used to model shared indicator variation. |
| Analysis of variance (ANOVA) | A method for studying mean differences through sources of variation. One-way ANOVA uses one grouping factor, and multi-way (factorial) ANOVA uses two or more crossed factors, as two-way and three-way ANOVA do; each factor can have several levels. |
| Fitted value | The value a fitted model assigns to an observed case. In a one-way group-mean model, it is that case's group mean. |
| Residual | An observed outcome minus its fitted value. A residual is calculated from the fitted model; an error is the corresponding unknown departure in the population model. |
| Mean square (MS) | A sum of squares divided by its degrees of freedom. In classical ANOVA, the within-group mean square estimates the common error variance under the model's conditions. |
| F statistic (F ratio) | In classical ANOVA, a ratio of the mean square for a tested source to the appropriate error mean square. Its null F reference depends on the model and both degrees of freedom. |
| Omnibus test | A test of one joint null hypothesis about a whole pattern, such as equality of all group means. Rejecting it does not identify which comparisons differ or how large they are. |
| Eta squared | The proportion of total observed variation attributed to a specified source in an ANOVA decomposition. In one-way ANOVA, it is between-group divided by total sum of squares. |
| Contrast (linear contrast) | A weighted combination of means whose weights sum to zero, expressing a specific comparison. The means, weights, and target population determine the quantity compared. |
| Familywise error rate (FWER) | The probability of at least one Type I error among a defined family of tests. Procedures such as Bonferroni allocate the error allowance across that family. |
| Simultaneous confidence intervals | A set of intervals calibrated so that, under their conditions, all of them cover their estimands together at the stated familywise rate; Bonferroni, Tukey, and Dunnett are different calibrations for different families. |
| Cell mean and marginal mean | In a two-factor layout, a cell mean is the mean of the cases sharing one level of each factor; a marginal mean averages the cell means across the levels of the other factor, with stated weights. |
| Main effect | A comparison across one factor's levels averaged over the other factor's levels, using stated weights. It remains an average when the conditional pattern differs across levels. |
| Interaction | A pattern in which a comparison across one factor's levels changes with the other factor's level. A difference of differences expresses one such comparison. |
| Simple effect | A comparison across one factor's levels at a specified level of the other factor. It describes a conditional comparison within the factorial design. |
| Three-way interaction (higher-order interaction) | A pattern in which a two-way interaction changes across the levels of a third factor. Each added factor multiplies the cells and adds interactions, so the highest-order interaction is read first and a few comparisons are declared in advance. |

: Selected concepts for group comparisons and ANOVA. {#tbl-ch04-key-terms tbl-colwidths="[28,72]"}

```{=latex}
\normalsize
```

### Exercise 4: Interpret comparison families (Integrative) {.unnumbered #ex-ch04-04}

In the invented background-sound study, thirty first-year students were
individually and randomly assigned to three sound conditions, ten to a
condition, and each answered the 0--20 comprehension quiz once after
reading the same passage. The group means are 12 for Silence, 10 for
Instrumental music and 8 for Music with lyrics. Under the independent
common-variance Normal model, $MS_W=178/27$ on 27 error df, so each
difference between two of these means has
$SE=\sqrt{(178/27)(1/10+1/10)}=1.148267616$; this SE and the critical
values below carry nine decimals so that the printed four-decimal
limits can be reproduced by hand. Two reports give the same estimate,
$-4$ comprehension points for Music with lyrics minus Silence, but the
comparison has a different history in each:

- **Report A.** Before any scores were seen, the study plan declared
  a family of two comparisons, each music condition against Silence:
  Instrumental music minus Silence and Music with lyrics minus Silence,
  with 95% simultaneous coverage for the pair.
- **Report B.** No comparison was declared in advance. After
  inspecting the three means, an analyst reports the largest pairwise
  difference, Music with lyrics minus Silence.

The Bonferroni critical value for two comparisons is 2.373417201, and
Report A's 95% simultaneous intervals are $[-4.7253,0.7253]$ for

## Appendix A: Deriving the Matched Pooled-t Identity {.unnumbered #app-ch04-pooled-identity}

[]{#app-ch04-calculations}

Section 2.4 states this identity and its conditions; the derivation
shows where it comes from. For two independent groups, let
$\widehat{\Delta\mu}=\bar y_1-\bar y_2$ and $N=n_1+n_2$. Their grand mean is

$$
\bar y=\frac{n_1\bar y_1+n_2\bar y_2}{N}.
$$

Subtracting it from each group mean gives

$$
\bar y_1-\bar y=\frac{n_2}{N}\widehat{\Delta\mu},
\qquad
\bar y_2-\bar y=-\frac{n_1}{N}\widehat{\Delta\mu}.
$$

Consequently,

$$
\begin{aligned}
SS_B
&=n_1\left(\frac{n_2}{N}\widehat{\Delta\mu}\right)^2
  +n_2\left(-\frac{n_1}{N}\widehat{\Delta\mu}\right)^2\\
&=\frac{n_1n_2}{N}\widehat{\Delta\mu}^2.
\end{aligned}
$$

There is one numerator df, so $MS_B=SS_B$. Define the pooled
variance $s_p^2=SS_W/(N-2)$, which is Chapter 3's pooled variance and
equals $MS_W$ when $J=2$. Because
$n_1n_2/N=1/(1/n_1+1/n_2)$,

$$
F=\frac{SS_B}{s_p^2}
=\frac{\widehat{\Delta\mu}^2}{s_p^2(1/n_1+1/n_2)}=t^2,
$$

where $t=\widehat{\Delta\mu}/\{s_p\sqrt{1/n_1+1/n_2}\}$ is the
equal-variance t statistic.

The equality is algebraic for these matched definitions; the equal
p-values add the test conditions and a two-sided t alternative. It
connects the one-way F test to the equal-variance t test of Chapter 3,
Section 5.3. The paired-samples t test (Chapter 3, Section 5.2) and
Welch's t test (Chapter 3, Section 5.4) have their own SEs and df, so
this algebra supplies neither; Welch's several-group counterpart is
the Welch one-way ANOVA of Section 5.2.

## Appendix B: Weighting and Effect-Size Reference {.unnumbered #app-ch04-comparisons}

### B.1 Unequal-cell weights {.unnumbered #app-ch04-weighting}

In the chapter's balanced data, equal-cell and student-weighted
marginal means coincide. For unequal cell counts, define them
separately:

$$
\bar y_{j\cdot}^{\text{students}}
=\frac{\sum_kn_{jk}\bar y_{jk}}{\sum_kn_{jk}},
\qquad
\bar y_{j\cdot}^{\text{equal cells}}
=\frac1K\sum_k\bar y_{jk}.
$$

The first describes the mixture of students observed in that
feedback group. The second gives each of the $K$ practice conditions
the same weight. Neither is automatically the right target for
every question.

For an illustration, retain Answer's cell means 8 and 12 but
imagine counts of 2 Massed and 6 Spaced students. The equally
weighted mean is $(8+12)/2=10$; the student-weighted mean is
$(2\times8+6\times12)/8=11$. These are hypothetical weights,
not changes to the actual four-per-cell dataset. A comparison of
feedback groups using different schedule mixtures can combine a
feedback comparison with a weighting difference. Adjusted means in
later chapters make their common profile or averaging distribution
explicit for this reason.

### B.2 Effect-size denominators {.unnumbered #app-ch04-effect-sizes}

Section 2.4 used one omnibus summary, eta squared. Software reports
several related summaries whose denominators differ, so each needs its
name and its denominator before it is interpreted.

\Needspace{14\baselineskip}

| Summary | Formula | Denominator | Value here |
|:--|:--|:--|--:|
| Eta squared, one-way | $SS_B/SS_T$ | All observed variation | .3101 |
| Omega squared, one-way | $\dfrac{SS_B-(J-1)MS_W}{SS_T+MS_W}$ | All observed variation plus one error mean square; the numerator first removes the variation expected from noise | .2525 |
| Eta squared for a factorial term | $SS_{\text{term}}/SS_T$ | All observed variation, including the other factors | Interaction .1345 |
| Partial eta squared | $\dfrac{SS_{\text{term}}}{SS_{\text{term}}+SS_E}$ | The term and the error only | Interaction .5161 |

: Four effect-size summaries and their denominators. {#tbl-ch04-effect-sizes tbl-colwidths="[24,25,37,14]"}

Here $\eta^2=80/258=.3101$, $\omega^2=\{80-2(178/27)\}/(258+178/27)=.2525$,
and the interaction's two summaries are $64/476=.1345$ and
$64/(64+60)=.5161$. Omega squared subtracts the between-group
variation that group means show even when the model means are equal;
it rests on the common-variance model, can fall below zero in a small
sample, and like eta squared says nothing about causation. The two
factorial rows show why the name matters: the same interaction is
.5161 of its partial denominator but .1345 of all the variation,
because the partial version leaves the feedback and practice
components out. In one-way ANOVA the two eta squared versions agree,
since the total holds only the factor and error. The raw mean
differences remain necessary for understanding the outcome scale.
